children.text: Built by a Spanish expedition in 1565, this was the first settlement fort in the Philippines, and today's stone bastion is counted as the oldest triangular bastion fort in the country. Its thick walls, cannons, garden courtyard and small museum can be seen in just over an hour.

Fort San Pedro is a triangular stone fort in downtown Cebu City, set on one side of Plaza Independencia right beside the harbor. It stands where the first Spanish settlement in the Philippines began, and it lets you see with your own eyes why Cebu is called "the oldest city in the Philippines." The stone fort you see today is said to date from around
, going by the year carved on the gate, and it is counted as the oldest triangular bastion fort in the country.
Its history goes back to

. Miguel López de Legazpi, who led the Spanish expedition, landed in Cebu and first built a wooden palisade to guard against attack; the fort is said to be named after his flagship, the San Pedro. The walls were rebuilt in stone in the early 17th century, and the form you see today took shape in the 18th century. The fort kept changing its face with each era: a defense post against Muslim raiders, a base for revolutionary forces in the 1898 Philippine Revolution, American army barracks, and a school under the Japanese occupation.

The layout is simple and handsome. Two sides face the sea and one faces the land, with a bastion at each corner. The southwest bastion is La Concepción, the southeast is Ignacio de Loyola, and the northeast is San Miguel; the walls are built of coral stone and limestone about
6m
high and

thick. Spanish-era cannons still point out to sea along the walls, and the roughly 2,000 ㎡ courtyard inside is laid out as a garden where you can rest in the shade even at midday. The fort is designated a National Cultural Treasure, and after the
earthquake damaged about 45% of the structure, it was restored at a cost of about
The fort is small, and a relaxed visit takes
1 hour 30 minutes–2 hours

. That makes it ideal as part of a half-day old-town walk together with Magellan's Cross and the Basilica of Santo Niño. It suits history lovers, photographers and families who want an easy outing, though the stairs and stone paving can be hard going for people with limited mobility.

blocks.title: Main gate arch and coat-of-arms relief

children.text: This is the land-side gate, the only way into the fort. Above the arch, the Spanish royal coat of arms and the name of the fort are carved in stone, and the Philippine flag flies from the wall above the gate. Take a front-on photo from the garden path in front of the gate, then step closer to look at the relief carved into the limestone.

blocks.title: Walking the walls and the three bastions

children.text: Climb the stairs onto the walls and walk the three bastions in turn. The highlights are the small stone turret on La Concepción Bastion, the cannons that once aimed at the sea, and the view down over the harbor and downtown from the top of the walls. Which sections are open depends on repair work, so follow the on-site notices.

Spanish colonial cannons sit along the walls and near the gate. Looking at the direction the muzzles point, you can immediately see how the fort guarded the harbor and the strait. The cannons are placed differently on each bastion, so compare them as you walk around.

blocks.title: The courtyard garden and the Cuerpo de Guardia

children.text: Inside the walls is a garden of lawn and tropical trees. The foundations of the former barracks and powder magazine remain beside the garden, and the garden and bastion areas can also be rented for weddings and events. With so much shade, it is the most comfortable place to take a break in the old town.

A building inside the fort displays Spanish-era documents, maps and artifacts, along with photographs and paintings showing how Cebu changed over time. A painting of Lapu-Lapu confronting Magellan's expedition at the Battle of Mactan stands out. Exhibits change from time to time, so follow the on-site notices.

blocks.title: Plaza Independencia and the Legazpi–Urdaneta Monument

children.text: The plaza right in front of the fort is a public space with a monument honoring Legazpi and Father Urdaneta. It is a good place to step out of the fort and look at the walls from outside, and beyond the plaza you can see boats coming and going at the pier.

blocks.title: Walking to Magellan's Cross and the Basilica of Santo Niño

children.text: Magellan's Cross and the Basilica of Santo Niño are about
northwest of the fort, roughly a
10-minute
walk. The starting points of Catholic history in the Philippines are gathered here, and seeing them together with the fort makes the story connect.

items.title: Half-day course
items.subtitle: The fort and an old-town walk

children.text: Enter the fort right after it opens. Early on it is cooler and quieter, which is good for photos of the main gate.
Look at the gate arch and the coat-of-arms relief, then go into the courtyard.
Climb the walls and see the three bastions of La Concepción, Ignacio de Loyola and San Miguel, and the cannons. Check on-site notices for which sections are open.
Visit the museum hall. See the Spanish-era documents and the painting of the Battle of Mactan.
Rest in the courtyard shade and look around the garden and the old barracks foundations.
Step out to Plaza Independencia, see the Legazpi–Urdaneta Monument and take a stroll.
Walk to Magellan's Cross and the Basilica of Santo Niño. You may not be able to enter the Magellan's Cross pavilion.
Finish with a lechon lunch in the city.
Walk along Colon Street, known as the oldest street in the Philippines.
Pick one museum that is open, such as the Casa Gorordo Museum or the National Museum of the Philippines in Cebu. Check opening days before you go.
Walk toward Carbon Market and browse snacks such as dried mangoes and sweets.
Head to Fuente Osmeña for street-grilled skewers for dinner.
Museums in the extension course differ in closing days and last-entry times, so keep the afternoon flexible.
It takes about
1 hour 20 minutes

from Manila to Mactan-Cebu International Airport (CEB), with Philippine Airlines and Cebu Pacific running several flights a day. From Korea there are direct flights from Incheon, Busan and other cities (about
4 hours 30 minutes
From the airport to the fort, a taxi takes about
40 minutes–1 hour 30 minutes
depending on traffic and costs about
. With Grab you know the fare in advance.
Within Cebu City, taxis and Grab are the easiest option. A single ride costs about
, and you can simply say "Plaza Independencia" or "Fort San Pedro" as your destination.
Traffic around Osmeña Boulevard is heavy from
5–8 PM
, so allow plenty of time.
A jeepney costs about
a ride and is cheap, but the routes are confusing. Jeepneys bound for Pier 1 pass near the fort, so tell the driver in advance where you want to get off.
Old-town sights such as Magellan's Cross, the Basilica of Santo Niño and Colon Street are each about
5–15 minutes
apart on foot, so it is easy to walk on from the fort.
The fort is right next to the Cebu port area, so it is easy to reach by boat. A fast ferry from Bohol takes about
2 hours
to reach the pier, and from the pier it is a short taxi ride to the fort.
A large ferry from Manila takes about
20–24 hours
, but schedules change often, so check the operator's notices before booking.
In Cebu City the dry season is
December–May
and the rainy season is more or less
June–November
. The fort is mostly outdoors, so it is best visited in the dry season, and
December–February
is especially pleasant because mornings and evenings are relatively cool for walking the walls. From
March–May
midday temperatures often exceed
and the shadeless wall tops heat up, so go right after opening or late in the afternoon.
Showers are frequent in the rainy season, and Cebu was badly hit by Typhoon Odette in
December 2021
. When a typhoon approaches the fort may close temporarily, so check announcements before you leave. During the Sinulog Festival around the third weekend of
January
, streets in the old town are closed and crowded, and getting around the fort takes much longer.

The fort is in the Cebu port area, so a downtown hotel near the old town is the most convenient base. Business and mid-range hotels cluster around Colon Street and Fuente Osmeña, at roughly
a night. If you want shopping and dining together, hotels around Ayala Center Cebu or IT Park (about
) are an option, though the fort is
15–30 minutes
away by taxi. You can also stay at a resort on Mactan Island near the airport and come into the city for only half a day.

The signature dish of Cebu is lechon, a whole pig roasted over charcoal until the skin is crisp. Cebu-style lechon is stuffed with seasonings and roasted, so it is tasty even without sauce. Eat it with puso, rice boiled in a woven palm-leaf pouch, and in the old town it is a good place to buy dried mangoes and sweets to take home. In the evening many travelers enjoy charcoal-grilled skewers at Larsian Barbecue near Fuente Osmeña. Inside the fort there is only a simple kiosk, so it is better to eat outside.
The fort closes before sunset, so it is safest to go in no later than
4 PM
. Opening hours differ between sources, so take
8 AM–5 PM
as a guide and confirm on site.
The stone paving on the walls is uneven and slippery after rain. Wear sneakers or sandals with firm soles.
Photos are best right after opening or when the sun is low. In morning light the limestone texture of the front gate shows up well.
The student and senior discount (about
) applies only if you show ID.
The fort is small and not a place to linger. Plan a half day combining it with Magellan's Cross, the Basilica of Santo Niño and Colon Street.
The sun is strong, so bring a hat, sunscreen and water, and rest in the courtyard shade as you go around.
The exhibit explanations are brief. Reading a little about Spanish settlement in Cebu beforehand makes the visit much richer.
Cathedrals and church areas require covered shoulders and knees, so dress accordingly if you plan to go on to one after the fort.
Fort San Pedro has been damaged by the
earthquake,
Typhoon Odette and the magnitude 6.9 Cebu earthquake of
September 30, 2025

, and right after the 2025 quake visits were suspended for a time for safety inspections. It is now receiving visitors, but some walls or buildings may be closed off temporarily for repair work, so check the latest notices from Cebu City Hall and the fort before you go.
Some stairs and walkways on the walls have low or no railings. Keep hold of children and do not stand at the edge.
Do not enter areas with construction screens or restricted-access signs. Stones may fall.

Outside the fort, around Plaza Independencia and the pier area, watch out for people who pose as guides and ask for money, and for pickpockets. Carry your bag in front and do not walk holding your phone in your hand.
Midday temperatures are often high, so watch for dehydration and heatstroke and drink water often.
The Magellan's Cross pavilion in the same area has had its entry restricted since cracks appeared in the
earthquake. Even if you cannot go inside, you can pray or offer candles from outside, so check the latest notices.
Ask for the taxi meter to be switched on, and if the driver refuses, use Grab instead.

by car, this gateway island of Cebu has the Lapu-Lapu monument from the Battle of Mactan, plus the airport and resorts.
About

by car from the city, this is a Greco-Roman style temple of love built on a hilltop in Busay.
About

by bus from the South Bus Terminal, this old town in southern Cebu keeps Spanish-era houses and churches.
